_note: The 20 hardest CA DMV written-test questions, ranked #1 = hardest ... #20 = easiest. Source: user-provided screenshots (Drivers Ed Direct countdown). The page renders easiest-first (#20 on top) counting down to #1. Explanations drafted for review.

questions.question: If there are two solid lines in the center of the roadway, you:

options.label: A
options.text: May cross the lines to turn left into a private driveway

options.label: B
options.text: Are on a two-lane one-way street

options.label: C
options.text: Should treat the lines as a solid wall and not cross for any reason

questions.explanation: Two solid lines mark a barrier you can't cross to pass another vehicle — but the law makes an exception for turning. You may cross them to turn left into or out of a driveway or private road. People assume "double solid = never cross," which is exactly why option C is the trap.

questions.question: You are approaching an uncontrolled intersection. You:

options.label: A
options.text: Must always stop before driving through the intersection

options.label: B
options.text: Should slow down and be ready to stop

options.label: C
options.text: Must yield the right-of-way to all other vehicles

questions.explanation: An uncontrolled intersection has no signs or signals, so you slow down and be ready to stop and yield. You don't have to come to a full stop every single time (A), and you don't automatically yield to everyone (C) — right-of-way depends on who arrived first and who's on the right.

questions.question: Which of these is a legal U-turn?

options.label: A
options.text: 150 feet away from a hill or curve

options.label: B
options.text: On a highway where there is an opening for a turn

options.label: C
options.text: Over two sets of double yellow lines in the roadway

questions.explanation: On a divided highway you may only make a U-turn where an opening is provided in the divider for turning. You can never cross two sets of double yellow lines to do it (C), and you must not U-turn on or near a hill or curve where other drivers can't see you — which is why A's framing is wrong.

questions.question: When is it legal to use a cell phone without a hands-free device while driving?

options.label: A
options.text: When making a call while stopped at a red light

options.label: B
options.text: Never

options.label: C
options.text: When making a call for emergency assistance

questions.explanation: Holding a phone while driving is illegal in California — the one exception is calling for emergency help (police, fire, or ambulance). Sitting at a red light still counts as driving (A), and "never" (B) ignores that emergency exception.

questions.question: What is the difference between traffic lights with red arrows and those with solid red lights?

options.label: A
options.text: Red arrows are only used to stop traffic which is turning left

options.label: B
options.text: You cannot turn on a red arrow, even if you stop first

options.label: C
options.text: Red arrows are only used for protected turn lanes

questions.explanation: A red arrow means stop and wait. Unlike a solid red light — where you can turn after stopping if it's legal — you may NOT turn on a red arrow even after coming to a complete stop. People who treat a red arrow like a normal red light are the ones who get caught.

questions.question: You are driving on a one-way street. You may turn left onto another one-way street:

options.label: A
options.text: Only if a sign permits the turn

options.label: B
options.text: If traffic on the street is moving to the right

options.label: C
options.text: If traffic on the street is moving to the left

questions.explanation: You can turn left from a one-way onto another one-way only when traffic on the street you're entering flows to the left. You don't need a special sign (A), and turning onto a street that flows right (B) would send you straight into oncoming traffic.

questions.question: Parking is NEVER permitted:

options.label: A
options.text: Twenty feet from a railroad track

options.label: B
options.text: In a crosshatched (diagonal) pattern space

options.label: C
options.text: In a bicycle lane, unless otherwise posted

questions.explanation: Crosshatched (diagonal-striped) areas are buffer zones — often beside disabled spaces — and parking there is never allowed. The other options have conditions (a distance, or "unless posted"), but a striped space is always off-limits.

questions.question: On freezing, wet days, which of the following roadways is most likely to hide spots of ice?

options.label: A
options.text: Roadways near the tops of hills

options.label: B
options.text: Roadways on bridges and overpasses

options.label: C
options.text: Roadways paved with asphalt

questions.explanation: Bridges and overpasses freeze first because cold air flows both above AND below the surface, so they lose heat faster than normal road. On a freezing, wet day they can hide ice even when the rest of the road just looks wet.

questions.question: If you are caught driving with a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) at or above the legal limit:

options.label: A
options.text: You may be fined by the court

options.label: B
options.text: Your breath test result by itself cannot be used to convict you

options.label: C
options.text: Your driver license will automatically be revoked

questions.explanation: A DUI conviction can bring court fines — on top of possible jail, a license suspension, and higher insurance. A breath test result absolutely can be used to convict you (B is false), and your license isn't revoked automatically on the spot; that goes through a DMV and court process (C overstates it).

questions.question: Other drivers are not making room for you to merge onto a freeway with heavy traffic. If necessary, you may:

options.label: A
options.text: Drive on the freeway shoulder until a gap appears

options.label: B
options.text: Stop before merging with freeway traffic

options.label: C
options.text: Make room by forcing your way into a small gap

questions.explanation: If there's truly no gap, it's better to stop at the end of the on-ramp and wait for a safe opening than to create a crash. You can't drive up the shoulder (A) or force your way into a gap that isn't there (C).

questions.question: You are driving on a road where the speed limit is 45 mph. All the other vehicles are driving 50 mph or faster. You may legally drive:

options.label: A
options.text: 50 mph or faster. The speed of traffic

options.label: B
options.text: Anywhere between 45 mph and 50 mph

options.label: C
options.text: No faster than 45 mph

questions.explanation: The posted limit is the legal maximum — "everyone else is speeding" doesn't make it legal for you. You may drive no faster than 45 mph here, even if traffic is flowing at 50+.

questions.question: You want to pass a bicyclist riding on the right edge of your lane. You:

options.label: A
options.text: Must not squeeze past the bicyclist

options.label: B
options.text: May not pass the bicyclist for any reason

options.label: C
options.text: Must honk your horn before passing the bicyclist

questions.explanation: If you can't give a cyclist at least 3 feet of space, you must not squeeze past inside the lane — slow down and wait or change lanes. You're allowed to pass when it's safe (so B is too extreme), and honking can startle a cyclist into a fall (C).

questions.question: You see a pedestrian with a white cane at the corner ready to cross the street. The person takes a step back and pulls in his cane. You should:

options.label: A
options.text: Stop your car a minimum of six feet from the crosswalk and wait for the person to cross the street

options.label: B
options.text: Stop. Proceed through the intersection. The person isn't ready to cross

options.label: C
options.text: Honk your horn to let the person know when to cross the street

questions.explanation: A pedestrian who pulls in the cane and steps back is signaling they are NOT crossing — so you may proceed when it's safe. People assume any white-cane user is about to step out, but here the body language means "go ahead." Never honk at a blind pedestrian; it can disorient them.

questions.question: If you are involved in a collision, you must exchange with the other person(s) involved, your driver license information and:

options.label: A
options.text: Proof of insurance only

options.label: B
options.text: Proof of insurance and vehicle registration only

options.label: C
options.text: Proof of insurance, vehicle registration, and current address

questions.explanation: Besides your driver-license info, you must exchange proof of insurance, vehicle registration, AND your current address. Almost everyone forgets the address — which is exactly what makes the "insurance only" and "insurance + registration" options wrong.

questions.question: After passing a car, it is safe to return to your driving lane when:

options.label: A
options.text: The driver you just passed signals you to return to your lane

options.label: B
options.text: You signal for three seconds your intention to return to your lane

options.label: C
options.text: You see the headlights of the passed car in your rearview mirror

questions.explanation: Once you can see the passed car's headlights in your rearview mirror, you've opened enough room to merge back without cutting them off. Don't wait for the other driver to wave you in (A) or rely on a 3-second signal alone (B) — the visible gap is the real cue.

questions.question: A white painted curb means:

options.label: A
options.text: Loading zone for freight or passengers

options.label: B
options.text: Loading zone for passengers or mail only

options.label: C
options.text: Loading zone for freight only

questions.explanation: White means a quick stop only — to load or unload passengers, or to drop off mail. Any answer that mentions freight is the trap, because loading freight belongs to yellow (commercial) zones.

questions.question: If you are towing another vehicle or trailer on a freeway with four lanes in your direction, you may travel in:

options.label: A
options.text: The far right lane only

options.label: B
options.text: Either of the two right lanes

options.label: C
options.text: Any of the traffic lanes in your direction

questions.explanation: Vehicles towing a trailer must keep right, but on a freeway with four or more lanes in your direction you may use either of the two right lanes — not just the far-right one. "Far right lane only" is the rule for narrower freeways, which is why most people pick it by mistake.

questions.question: Where should you stop your vehicle if there is no crosswalk or limit line?

options.label: A
options.text: Just past the corner

options.label: B
options.text: At the corner

options.label: C
options.text: Twenty feet before the corner

questions.explanation: With no painted crosswalk or limit (stop) line, you stop at the corner — the edge of the intersection, before entering it. "Twenty feet before" sounds official but isn't a real rule, and stopping just past the corner puts you into cross traffic.

questions.question: Even if you know your vehicle can maneuver a sharp curve at the legal speed limit, you should still slow down because:

options.label: A
options.text: There may be a stalled car or a collision ahead that you cannot see

options.label: B
options.text: You must legally drive below the speed limit on sharp curves

options.label: C
options.text: The strong inward pull on your vehicle can be dangerous

questions.explanation: A curve blocks your view of the road, so you slow down in case there's a stalled car, debris, or a crash just out of sight. There's no blanket law forcing you below the limit on every curve (B), and the wording in C is wrong — the force in a curve pushes you outward, not inward.

questions.question: At an uncontrolled intersection where you can't see cross traffic until you are just about to enter the intersection, the speed limit is:

options.label: A
options.text: 15 mph

options.label: B
options.text: 25 mph

options.label: C
options.text: 20 mph

questions.explanation: At a blind intersection — where you can't see 100 feet in each direction during the last 100 feet before crossing — the limit drops to 15 mph. Teens default to the 25 mph residential limit, but limited visibility lowers it.
